subject: principles-of-accounts
title: Absorption and Marginal Costing: Where the Fixed Overhead Goes

questions.prompt: A business produces 1,000 units and sells 800. Fixed production overhead is $12,000. Why does absorption costing report a higher profit than marginal costing here?

choices.text: It does not - both methods always report the same profit because fixed overhead is a period cost under both
Absorption costing attaches $12 per unit to inventory, so the 200 unsold units carry $2,400 of fixed overhead forward instead of charging it to this period
Absorption costing ignores fixed production overhead completely
Marginal costing double-counts the fixed production overhead

questions.misconception: Absorption and marginal costing always report the same profit, because fixed production overhead is a period cost under both methods.
questions.explanation: The trap claim is: Absorption and marginal costing always report the same profit, because fixed production overhead is a period cost under both methods. In fact The methods differ on timing: marginal costing expenses the full $12,000 of fixed production overhead in the period, but absorption costing attaches $12 per unit to inventory, so the 200 unsold units carry 200 x $12 = $2,400 of fixed overhead forward in closing inventory - which is why absorption profit of $9,400 exceeds marginal profit of $7,000 by exactly that $2,400 deferral.

questions.prompt: What are the marginal and absorption unit costs when direct materials are $10, direct labour $6, variable overhead $4 and fixed overhead $12 per unit?
questions.explanation: Scene 1 and scene 2 work this: both methods include the three variable layers ($10 + $6 + $4 = $20); only absorption adds the $12 fixed overhead layer, giving $32.

questions.prompt: A student claims the two methods must give the same profit because the fixed overhead is the same $12,000 either way. Explain, in two sentences, why the profits differ when production exceeds sales.
questions.answer: The methods differ on timing: marginal costing expenses the full $12,000 of fixed production overhead in the period, but absorption costing attaches $12 per unit to inventory, so the 200 unsold units carry 200 x $12 = $2,400 of fixed overhead forward in closing inventory - which is why absorption profit of $9,400 exceeds marginal profit of $7,000 by exactly that $2,400 deferral.
questions.explanation: The deciding habit is to follow the timing: the $12,000 is identical, but absorption costing defers the share attached to unsold units into closing inventory while marginal costing charges it all to the period.

questions.prompt: In one sentence, state how much fixed overhead is carried forward in closing inventory and how it is calculated.
questions.answer: Closing inventory of 200 units carries 200 x $12 = $2,400 of fixed overhead forward under absorption costing.
questions.explanation: Scene 3 shows the deferral directly: unsold units times the fixed overhead absorbed per unit.

questions.prompt: Which list gives the profit reconciliation in order?

choices.text: Marginal profit $7,000, plus fixed overhead deferred in closing inventory 200 x $12 = $2,400, equals absorption profit $9,400
Marginal profit $9,400, plus $2,400, equals absorption profit $7,000
Marginal profit $7,000, plus the full $12,000 of fixed overhead, equals absorption profit $9,400
Both profits are $7,000, so there is nothing to reconcile

questions.explanation: Scene 4 reconciles the bars: the only difference between the two profit figures is the $2,400 of fixed overhead deferred in closing inventory.
